question: A 53-year-old man comes to the emergency department for severe left knee pain for the past 8 hours. He describes it as an unbearable, burning pain that woke him up from his sleep. He has been unable to walk since. He has not had any trauma to the knee. Ten months ago, he had an episode of acute pain and swelling of the right great toe that subsided after treatment with indomethacin. He has hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, psoriasis, and hyperlipidemia. Current medications include topical betamethasone, metformin, glipizide, losartan, and simvastatin. Two weeks ago, hydrochlorothiazide was added to his medication regimen to improve blood pressure control. He drinks 1–2 beers daily. He is 170 cm (5 ft 7 in) tall and weighs 110 kg (242 lb); BMI is 38.1 kg/m2. His temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F). Examination shows multiple scaly plaques over his palms and soles. The left knee is erythematous, swollen, and tender; range of motion is limited by pain. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Psoriasis -> increased risk of psoriatic arthritis -> possible cause of left knee pain -> 70% CHAIN: Hyperuricemia -> gout flare -> possible cause of left knee pain -> 60% CHAIN: Acute gout flare -> responds to NSAIDs -> possible treatment with colchicine -> 70% CHAIN: Acute gout flare -> may present with erythema, swelling, and tenderness -> consistent with left knee examination findings -> 80% CHAIN: Acute gout flare -> may require joint fluid analysis -> consideration for arthrocentesis -> 70%
enhanced_information: The most appropriate next step in management for the 53-year-old man with severe left knee pain and a history of psoriasis, hyperuricemia, and acute gout flare is arthrocentesis to evaluate for acute gout flare. The examination findings of erythema, swelling, and tenderness in the left knee are consistent with acute gout flare, which responds to NSAIDs and may require joint fluid analysis. Serum uric acid level testing may also be considered to further support the diagnosis.
analysis: The core medical principle in this case is to evaluate for acute gout flare given the patient's history of hyperuricemia, psoriasis, and acute gout flare in the past. The enhanced information supports the need for arthrocentesis to confirm the diagnosis of acute gout flare. While serum uric acid level testing could be considered, arthrocentesis is more definitive in this acute presentation. Oral colchicine may be initiated after confirming the diagnosis. Intra-articular triamcinolone and oral methotrexate are not the initial management for acute gout flare.
